title: Central European mine pumping and remote mechanical power
summary: Mines used a portfolio of human, animal and water power; remote rod transmission expanded the usable hydraulic choice set without requiring steam.

stages.invention: Multiple devices predate the interval; exact priority for crank/rod combinations is disputed, not fixed here.
stages.feasibility: Agricola gives operating descriptions; later scholarship compares feasible direct and remote-drive arrangements.
stages.deployment: Named mine accounts and later depictions support installations; drawings alone are not a census.
stages.diffusion: Continued descriptions and installations provide qualitative evidence; no denominator established.
stages.scaling: Remote transmission allowed a stream to serve distant pumps; scale in total regional output unresolved.
stages.non-adoption: Site water, transmission expense and maintenance constrained individual choices; no general hydraulic absence inferred.
stages.displacement: Human, horse and hydraulic devices coexisted; no complete replacement date established.

counterevidence: First-use dates and prevalence are uncertain; celebratory images can be selective; adequate hydraulics delaying steam remains a hypothesis.

episode.technology_configuration: Direct and remote-drive hydraulic mine pumps, alongside human and animal devices; direct pumps and later remote rod work are explicit subepisodes.
episode.task: Remove water and raise mine loads sufficiently to continue extraction.
episode.population: Selected central European mines described by Agricola and later technical authors and represented in mining imagery; not all German mines.
contemporary_alternatives: Direct hydraulic pumps where streams could be diverted
Drainage tunnels or foregoing deeper extraction
episode.adoption_measure: Qualitative descriptions, named installations and later depictions; no verified total installation denominator.
episode.observation_limits: Treatises select remarkable machinery; artistic depictions may conflate arrangements. Availability of a description is not evidence of a region-wide installed stock.

actors.chooser: Mine owners, investors and technical managers, as described by treatises; precise governance differs by mine.
actors.payer: Owners and shareholders supply resources; Agricola describes contributions but no comparative capital accounts audited here.
actors.operator_maintainer: Mine workers, pump attendants, smiths and carpenters; task descriptions exist but occupation-specific earnings not established.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Miners whose work depends on drainage, hauling labourers, and downstream water users; effects on the latter unmeasured.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Agricola says workers may leave when provisioning raises required wages, but this prescription is not a labour-mobility census. Authority and miners’ actual refusal rights remain uncertain.

labour.tasks: Hauling, tending water supply, maintaining chains, rods and pump components; human prime-moving effort could be reorganised rather than eliminated.
labour.entry_barriers: Mechanical craft skills, access to materials and mine finance; exact apprenticeship routes and exclusion unknown.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Owners allocate capital; treatise acknowledges provisioning and wage demands. Actual division of gains is not measured.
labour.transition: Later descriptions indicate changes over decades; no followed worker or cohort transition.
labour.distribution: No verified group-specific earnings or welfare series. Heavy machinery introduced hazards as well as reduced hauling requirements.
labour.evidence_limit: Sources are strongest on apparatus and stated decision criteria, weak on workers’ options, incomes and displacement rates.

title: Coalfield and Cornish steam pumping, fuel economy and collective improvement
summary: A fuel-intensive drainage technology occupied an early niche; fuel economy, information sharing and local financing changed viable applications.

stages.invention: Newcomen’s workable atmospheric engine and Watt’s condenser are distinct stages; later high-pressure designs were further changes.
stages.feasibility: Atmospheric operation fitted early engineering capability; improved economy mattered in high-coal-cost Cornwall.
stages.deployment: Boulton and Watt erected Cornish pumping engines; original installation records accessed through Nuvolari.
stages.diffusion: Mine district reporting from 1811 supported comparisons; not a national count of all engines.
stages.scaling: Incremental efficiency and expanded investment accompanied district improvements; aggregate early steam impact remained small in Crafts’s accounting.
stages.non-adoption: Fuel cost could make early engines unattractive away from cheap-coal locations; engineering and royalties also mattered.
stages.displacement: Alternative compound and single-cylinder designs persisted; no universal extinction of earlier pumps inferred.

counterevidence: Patent expiry, reporting, high-pressure engines and investment were not independent shocks; duty is not mine profit.

episode.technology_configuration: Atmospheric coalfield pumping and fuel-efficient Cornish pumping, then post-1811 reporting and incremental improvement; these are separate local phases.
episode.task: Keep mines drained at acceptable total operating cost.
episode.population: Selected British coalfield applications and Cornish mining engines/investors; macro steam accounting is a separate aggregate comparison.
episode.adoption_measure: Nuvolari’s installation narrative and comparative engine-duty series; Crafts’s reconstructed horsepower and growth accounting are not the same population.
episode.observation_limits: Original contracts and Lean reports are inherited through scholarship; best reported duty may differ from typical annual performance.

actors.chooser: Mine adventurers and captains choose and commission engines; engineers offer designs and operational alterations.
actors.payer: Mine investors pay installations and royalties; Boulton and Watt receive contracted fuel-saving premiums.
actors.operator_maintainer: Engineers, enginemen and pump crews; operational and minor maintenance changes enter reported performance.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Miners, engine workers, local communities and coal suppliers; welfare effects not independently measured.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Investors could dispute contracts or order rival engines, subject to patents and courts. Workers’ consent to engine change is not established by owner purchasing evidence.

labour.tasks: Pumping labour and fuel handling reorganised; engine erection, maintenance, adjustment and performance comparison became important tasks.
labour.entry_barriers: Engineering knowledge, reputation and access to capital; no complete entry or apprenticeship series.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Patentees sought royalty income; mine shareholders and managers coordinated expenditure; engineers competed in reported performance.
labour.transition: Patent expiry, slack maintenance and later reporting are sequential, but individual careers and displaced-worker absorption are unknown.
labour.distribution: Investor and engineer incentives are described; no representative wage, mortality or livelihood effect is estimated.
labour.evidence_limit: Duty measures useful mechanical work per fuel, not net profit or worker welfare; royalty disputes are not a causal estimate of patent policy.

title: British textile mills choosing water, steam and collective reservoirs
summary: Local water scarcity, mixed-power operation and unbuilt reservoir schemes challenge a single national energy-price account.

stages.invention: The relevant choice involved existing prime movers and proposed infrastructure, not a new first invention.
stages.feasibility: Hydrological potential differs from dependable and legally accessible power; reservoir technical feasibility is not audited here.
stages.deployment: Steam sometimes supplemented or recirculated water before replacing it.
stages.diffusion: The 1838 factory return and mill-location reconstruction indicate geographical variation, not uniform British adoption.
stages.scaling: Concentrated mills could exceed convenient local water supply; collective reservoirs were a possible but contingent response.
stages.non-adoption: Malm attributes non-realisation of major reservoir proposals partly to coordination requirements; abstract-only attribution.
stages.displacement: Steam gained in cotton districts while water remained viable elsewhere; no single national replacement moment.

counterevidence: Run-of-river reconstruction does not price reservoirs or determine initial industrial geography. Abstract-only access limits the coordination account.

episode.technology_configuration: Water-driven textile mills, steam supplementation or replacement, and proposed collective reservoirs; built mixed systems and unbuilt proposals are distinguished.
episode.task: Provide sufficient dependable mill power while retaining viable production locations.
episode.population: British textile mills with emphasis on Greater Manchester/Mersey; reservoir promoters and potential subscribers are a different observed subgroup.
episode.interval: c. 1780–1850, with 1838 factory evidence a benchmark
episode.adoption_measure: Factory-return power requirements combined with geographic reconstruction; reservoir outcomes qualitative and abstract-only.
episode.observation_limits: Theoretical water potential is not priced dependable capacity. Proposal existence is not operational feasibility or adoption.

actors.chooser: Mill owners, reservoir promoters and owners/users of water rights.
actors.payer: Individual manufacturers or proposed collective subscribers; detailed project finance not inspected.
actors.operator_maintainer: Mill engineers and workers maintain engines, wheels and transmission; reservoir operation would require additional coordination.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Factory workers, neighbouring water users and communities exposed to emissions; impacts not quantified here.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Manufacturers could decline subscription; evidence for workers choosing power sources is absent. Rights holders and collective agreements could constrain owner choices.

labour.tasks: Power tending and maintenance differ across systems; existing labour access may influence site retention, but this study does not quantify that motive.
labour.entry_barriers: Finance, land/water rights, engineering competence; comparative worker entry barriers unknown.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Individual engine ownership contrasts with proposed shared water infrastructure; worker bargaining evidence not acquired.
labour.transition: Mixed systems show partial conversion; no labour cohorts followed across power changes.
labour.distribution: Fuel and coordination costs affect owners; no inference of improved worker autonomy from dependable power.
labour.evidence_limit: Hydrology cannot identify labour-control motives, and the abstract-only reservoir source cannot establish scheme-level distributive effects.

title: British spinning, factory organisation and machine-tool complements
summary: Task-specific pay, product demands, power, precision machinery and control over work need separation when explaining mechanisation.

stages.invention: Jennies, water frames and later mules/tools are distinct inventions; exact firsts and all development costs not reconstructed.
stages.feasibility: Repeatable operation required appropriate craft and engineering capabilities; small devices and complex machinery differed.
stages.deployment: Factory machinery and outwork were contemporary alternatives; Ure records managerial advocacy rather than a deployment census.
stages.diffusion: Displacement of hand spinning is established qualitatively in scholarship, with different fibre and regional trajectories.
stages.scaling: Machine tools and replacement parts supported repeated machine supply; labour recruitment and organisation remained necessary.
stages.non-adoption: Extending outwork or importing yarn could address capacity needs without immediate factory concentration.
stages.displacement: Hand-spinning income contracted while engineering skill demand expanded; complete deskilling is not inferred.

counterevidence: Most hand-spinning pay observations concern wool; cotton time-use data are scarce. An anti-high-wage finding does not identify one alternative motive.

episode.technology_configuration: Hand spinning/outwork versus mechanised spinning and factory organisation, with later machinery production and repair as a linked engineering subepisode.
episode.task: Produce yarn of suitable quantity and quality, and reproducibly supply the machinery that does so.
episode.population: British spinners across several fibres in archival pay records; advocates and engineering accounts concern partly different cotton-factory and machinery populations.
episode.interval: c. 1760–1850; wage reconstruction also reaches earlier years
episode.adoption_measure: Pay observations, factory/engineering descriptions and qualitative displacement; no common national adoption denominator.
episode.observation_limits: Cotton observations are scarce in wage data dominated by wool; retrospective machinery histories and pro-factory testimony are not representative worker surveys.

actors.chooser: Yarn masters, factory owners and machine producers; some household producers make smaller-scale choices.
actors.payer: Owners and investors finance equipment/materials; households contribute labour and sometimes tools.
actors.operator_maintainer: Women and children in hand and factory tasks, skilled spinners, mechanics and instrument/tool makers; composition varies with process.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Dependent hand-spinning households and children recruited under institutional arrangements; these are not equivalent to free investor purchasers.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Poor-law, prison and household dependence qualify voluntariness; Ure’s aspiration for tractable labour does not establish actual refusal rights for all factories.

labour.tasks: Hand yarn work displaced or reorganised; machine tending, fitting, precision metalwork and repair expanded. Paid and household work coexist.
labour.entry_barriers: Engineering and skilled operative training, machinery assets and gendered access to occupations; no complete transition matrix.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Yarn masters often controlled fibre and wages; factory owners controlled capital; mechanics could retain skills and organisation despite deskilling aspirations.
labour.transition: A multi-decade change with different fibres and tasks; no evidence that the same displaced spinners became mechanics.
labour.distribution: Evidence documents low spinners’ pay and managerial substitution motives; aggregate output gains cannot establish compensation of displaced women.
labour.evidence_limit: The sources do not estimate lifetime losses, child welfare or a causal skill premium; pay comparisons require careful time and task units.

title: India–Lancashire competition, colonial markets and uneven displacement
summary: Productivity, cotton/freight prices, domestic political and agricultural shocks, slavery-linked demand and asymmetric policy power offer interacting explanations.

stages.invention: This case evaluates competitive diffusion and displacement rather than identifying a first machine.
stages.feasibility: British machinery could be feasible without immediately undercutting every Indian product after input and delivery costs.
stages.deployment: British mechanised output reached different export markets at different times; Indian manufacture predated this competition.
stages.diffusion: Trade and price reconstructions track competitive shifts; they are not uniform adoption rates for Indian producers.
stages.scaling: Expanding markets and raw-material supply interacted with machine productivity; colonial market access was politically shaped.
stages.non-adoption: Low wages alone are not accepted as a sufficient explanation for Indian production choices; capital and policy constraints need further study.
stages.displacement: Hand-spinning, export production, handloom weaving and later mill growth require separate series; universal destruction of handicrafts is not claimed.

counterevidence: National aggregate estimates and wage units are fragile; a cost advantage does not identify market formation, and a coercive policy does not identify every product’s counterfactual.

episode.technology_configuration: Indian artisanal textile supply and Lancashire mechanised competition through different markets; early cost competition and later colonial import penetration are explicit subepisodes.
episode.task: Sell cotton yarn/cloth of specified quality and obtain livelihood or merchant profit.
episode.population: Reconstructed British/Indian trade, wages and prices; regional producers are aggregated imperfectly. India is not treated as one factory or a homogeneous chooser.
episode.interval: c. 1700–1900, with model phase distinctions around 1810 and later mill growth
contemporary_alternatives: Indian hand-produced export and local cloth
Protective policy where political authority permitted it
episode.adoption_measure: Trade flows, relative prices, employment reconstructions and qualitative market change; loss of export share is not a technology-adoption denominator.
episode.observation_limits: Quality, task and household labour units differ; aggregate shares can change because foreign output expands. Colonial records have administrative selection.

actors.chooser: British and Indian producers and merchants choose production/sourcing within constraints; British/Company political authorities shape trade rules.
actors.payer: Producers, investors and trading firms fund production; enslaved producers and dependent households bear labour costs not reducible to voluntary capital supply.
actors.operator_maintainer: Spinners, weavers, dyers, factory workers and mechanics across distinct systems.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Indian textile households, enslaved Atlantic commodity producers, and subjects without equivalent tariff sovereignty.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Colonial subjects lacked symmetric authority over trade policy; enslaved labour was coerced. Individual artisans’ practical exit options and contract restrictions require regional study.

labour.tasks: Spinning, weaving and finishing faced different technical shocks; some labour shifted activities while later mills created different jobs.
labour.entry_barriers: Machine finance, raw materials, technical services, merchant access and occupational institutions; their separate effects remain unmeasured.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Imperial authorities shaped protection; merchants and owners controlled market access. Household earnings cannot be equated with an individual male wage.
labour.transition: Models distinguish phases, but lack sufficient person-level data to track displaced families into later occupations.
labour.distribution: Decline differs by task and locality; no claim that later growth compensated earlier households or that imported cheap cloth settled the welfare balance.
labour.evidence_limit: Competing reconstructions do not identify a unique colonial, climate or wage contribution; original fiscal and household records remain necessary.

title: Rings, mules and adaptation in Japan, India and Britain
summary: Imported spinning equipment was recombined with local cotton preparation, labour and skills; machine rankings changed over time.

stages.invention: Ring and mule lineages predate the main comparison; high drafting later changed fibre control.
stages.feasibility: Product count, fibre length, preparation and operatives affected workable use.
stages.deployment: Supplier orders establish purchases; installation and realised utilisation are incompletely observed.
stages.diffusion: The study follows major British exporters’ records across countries, with defined coverage limits.
stages.scaling: Japanese mixed-cotton preparation expanded ring capability; supplier improvements widened the range of adopters.
stages.non-adoption: Mule purchases continued where skill and flexibility conferred advantages; this need not indicate stagnation.
stages.displacement: Ring gains and high drafting eroded mule applications in the 1920s; specialised persistence continued and is not reduced to a single switch date.

counterevidence: Orders and specifications differ from output; adoption regressions are not exogenous identification; Indian labour-relations explanation is explicitly tentative.

episode.technology_configuration: Rings and mules in international orders, Japanese cotton-mixing package in the 1890s, and Indian high-draft orders in 1929–1933 are distinct subepisodes.
episode.task: Spin desired yarn counts reliably from available cotton at viable cost.
episode.population: Customers of major British spinning-machinery exporters; country aggregates of specified orders, not every mill or spindle.
contemporary_alternatives: Mule spinning with specific operative skills
Different fibre mixtures and preparation work
episode.adoption_measure: Supplier order types and specifications; selected national installed-spindle tables are a different measure. No direct profit or worker-welfare measure.
episode.observation_limits: Orders may differ from completed installations or usage; cotton specification is missing for some orders; buyers unable to finance any machine are underobserved.

actors.chooser: Mill management chooses equipment with machinery suppliers’ advice; recruitment and cotton buying are coordinated managerial decisions.
actors.payer: Mill owners/investors; precise national financing constraints not reconstructed.
actors.operator_maintainer: Mule spinners with maintenance skills, ring attendants, cotton-preparation workers and mechanics; gender composition differs across the episodes.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Workers allocated machines, pace and tasks; families supplying young workers.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Purchasing records establish employer choice, not workers’ consent. Source indicates organised/skill-based mule labour and young female recruitment, but does not supply a comparative freedom-to-exit audit.

labour.tasks: Mixing and fibre preparation could use more labour while machine tending changed; mule skills included adjustment and maintenance.
labour.entry_barriers: Tacit mule skills and apprenticeship-like learning versus less experienced ring workforces; access to mill capital and imports remains necessary.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Management and supplier choices interact with organised skilled labour and workforce composition; Indian explanation remains tentative.
labour.transition: Country-level technical change is observed for decades, but individual occupational mobility is not.
labour.distribution: Output potential and labour use are studied; no reliable comparative wages, hours or health outcomes for the affected groups established here.
labour.evidence_limit: Technical progress in machine orders must not be translated into freedom, welfare or an inherent national labour quality.

title: Chinese household weaving and factory-yarn hybrids
summary: Factory yarn could displace hand spinning and support handloom weaving; household work also carried gendered meanings and constraints.

stages.invention: Neither factory yarn nor the handloom is a new invention in this interval.
stages.feasibility: Different yarn characteristics supported selective combination of factory warp and hand-spun weft.
stages.deployment: Named districts and historical accounts describe hybrid use; exact household installations are not enumerated.
stages.diffusion: Eyferth reports continuing handloom output and spread with yarn access; underlying original surveys were not audited.
stages.scaling: Machine intermediates could extend hand production geographically, rather than only displace it.
stages.non-adoption: Cash, alternative earnings, product requirements and gender arrangements are candidate constraints; preferences cannot be inferred from persistence alone.
stages.displacement: Spinning declined faster than hand weaving; reported 1934–1936 handloom output share remains substantial.

counterevidence: Main source studies a later period and uses earlier scholarship for this background. National quantities are estimates; post-1949 mechanisms are not projected backward.

episode.technology_configuration: Household hand weaving with machine-spun warp and/or hand-spun weft; regional factory-yarn access and gendered work classification.
episode.task: Provide cloth with practical and social uses while sustaining household livelihoods.
episode.population: Selected Chinese weaving districts and national estimates reported through earlier scholarship; household cases are not uniformly represented.
contemporary_alternatives: Purchased factory yarn with hand weaving
Different fibres or reduced clothing consumption
episode.adoption_measure: Reported cotton-output share for handloom cloth and qualitative hybrid-use accounts; not a census of technology preferences.
episode.observation_limits: Pre-1949 evidence is background in a mainly post-1949 study; underlying earlier studies not independently inspected; unpaid work is often poorly recorded.

actors.chooser: Household decision-makers, merchants and women producing cloth, with authority distributed unequally and not fully observed.
actors.payer: Households supply cash/materials and unpaid or undercounted labour; merchants may mediate inputs and sales.
actors.operator_maintainer: Predominantly women doing spinning, weaving and household textile work, with actual regional divisions more diverse than ideals.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Women and girls whose time can be allocated by household norms; dependants requiring clothing.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Persistence does not demonstrate freely chosen preference; gender prescriptions and limited cash or outside work may constrain refusal. Exact household bargaining is unknown.

labour.tasks: Hand spinning contracted unevenly; weaving could persist using industrial inputs; paid market and unpaid household production overlapped.
labour.entry_barriers: Embodied textile skills, access to cotton/yarn and looms, gendered expectations and alternative employment access.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Household and merchant relations shape resource access; the article’s discourse evidence does not identify each woman’s control of proceeds.
labour.transition: Regional coexistence and interwar shares observed; no tracked cohort of spinners transitioning to factory employment.
labour.distribution: Women’s work could be economically consequential yet omitted from reformers’ definitions; no full pre-1949 time or wage distribution established.
labour.evidence_limit: Post-1949 rationing findings cannot establish pre-1949 causation; national output estimates cannot settle household welfare.

title: US manufacturing electrification and factory redesign
summary: Line-shaft replacement, group drive and unit drive were distinct arrangements; electricity service and machine redesign shaped their value.

stages.invention: Electric motors and generation preceded broad industrial reorganisation; exact first-use claims are not needed here.
stages.feasibility: Reliable motor operation did not establish machine compatibility or economic superiority in every factory.
stages.deployment: Early motors often retained existing shafts; group and unit configurations followed and coexisted.
stages.diffusion: Motor horsepower shares are documented; unit-drive prevalence is inferred from technical sources, not comprehensively counted.
stages.scaling: Utility networks, equipment suppliers, installation advice and new factory design helped expansion.
stages.non-adoption: Existing onsite generation and group operations could make immediate conversion unattractive.
stages.displacement: Mechanical distribution was reduced over time; electric motors could still rely on steam-generated electricity.

counterevidence: Engineering-focused sources underrepresent workers; aggregate productivity gains are not all independently assigned to electrification.

episode.technology_configuration: Electric line-shaft retrofits, group drive and unit drive in US factories, with onsite versus utility generation separately identified.
episode.task: Deliver controllable mechanical work and organise production economically.
episode.population: US manufacturing mechanical-drive capacity and selected factories described in technical literature; no comprehensive unit-drive census.
episode.adoption_measure: Electric motor horsepower share, approximately 25% in 1909 and over 53% in 1919; unit-drive prevalence inferred qualitatively from design and technical literature.
episode.observation_limits: Capacity is not actual utilisation, output or establishment count; engineering sources select projects and suppliers’ promotional successes.

actors.chooser: Factory owners/managers, production engineers and utility/supplier advisers.
actors.payer: Manufacturers finance equipment; utilities finance networks and sometimes lend motors or installation assistance.
actors.operator_maintainer: Machine operatives, electricians, mechanics, utility operators and production planners.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Workers whose pace and discretion change; communities affected by power generation; neither outcome well measured here.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Owners can retain installed equipment; workers’ consent to changed work organisation is not established. Customer choice among power arrangements differs from operator autonomy.

labour.tasks: Belt adjustment and mechanical distribution maintenance reduced; motor installation, electrical maintenance and production reorganisation expanded.
labour.entry_barriers: Electrical/engineering competence and factory investment; credential and demographic access not reconstructed.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Owners and utilities control capital and power service; evidence does not quantify workers’ share of productivity gains.
labour.transition: Multiple configurations coexist through decades; no linked worker-career dataset.
labour.distribution: Potential efficiency and control gains are documented; no inference of improved wages, pace, safety or autonomy for every worker.
labour.evidence_limit: Engineering and horsepower data cannot identify livelihoods or allocate all productivity gains to electrification.
